incidente.resumo: While manually re-synchronising a lagging PostgreSQL secondary for GitLab.com, a wipe of the database directory was executed on the primary instead of the secondary, removing around 300 GB of data; GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours and database changes made after 17:20 UTC on January 31 were lost. Backups proved unusable, so service was restored by copying a 6-hour-old LVM snapshot-based staging database to production and restoring webhooks from a separate copy.

descricao.texto: The process was terminated a second or two after the mistake was noticed by the engineer running it, by which time around 300 GB of data had been removed.
trechos: The engineer terminated the process a second or two after noticing their mistake, but at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.

gatilho.texto: While trying to restore replication, a wipe of the PostgreSQL database directory, intended for the secondary, was executed on the primary instead; around 300 GB of data had been removed before the process was terminated.
trechos: Trying to restore the replication process, an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary.
Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead.
The engineer terminated the process a second or two after noticing their mistake, but at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.

descricao.texto: After replication stopped, rebuilding the secondary required an empty PostgreSQL data directory, and this re-synchronisation was manual work that was neither automated nor properly documented.
trechos: 2. **Why was the database directory removed?** - Database replication stopped,
requiring the secondary to be reset/rebuilt. This in turn requires that the
PostgreSQL data directory is empty. Restoring this required manual work as
this was not automated, nor was it documented properly.

Unfortunately DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, resulting in them being rejected by the receiver.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers, as the other backup procedures were assumed sufficient, and the secondary's data had already been wiped, so neither host could be used for recovery.
trechos: While enabled for the NFS servers, these snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers as we assumed that our other backup procedures were sufficient enough.
At this point the replication process was broken and data had already been wiped from both the primary and secondary, meaning we could not restore from either host.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The staging environment used Azure classic without Premium Storage; its network disks were throttled to around 60Mbps, so copying the data from staging to production took around 18 hours.
trechos: For our staging environment we were using Azure classic, without Premium Storage.
Copying the data from the staging to the production host took around 18 hours.
These disks are network disks and are throttled to a really low number (around 60Mbps), there is no way to move from cheap storage to premium, so this was the performance we would get out of it.

passos.texto: The LVM snapshot created about 6 hours before the outage was chosen for recovery; the PostgreSQL data directory was copied from the staging host to production (around 18 hours), and the database was restored to its state at January 31st, 17:20 UTC.
trechos: To recover GitLab.com we decided to use the LVM snapshot created 6 hours before the outage, as it was our only option to reduce data loss as much as possible (the alternative was to lose almost 24 hours of data).
Since copying over and restoring the data directory would be easier we decided to go with this solution.
Copying the data from the staging to the production host took around 18 hours.
Once copied we were able to restore the database (including webhooks) to the state it was at January 31st, 17:20 UTC.

passos.texto: On February 1st at 17:00 UTC the GitLab.com database was restored without webhooks; webhooks were restored by creating a separate staging database from the LVM snapshot without triggering webhook removal, generating a SQL dump of the table and importing it, with final restoration finished around 18:00 UTC.
trechos: On February 1st at 17:00 UTC we managed to restore the GitLab.com database without webhooks.
Restoring webhooks was done by creating a separate staging database using the LVM snapshot, but without triggering the removal of webhooks.
This allowed us to generate a SQL dump of the table and import this into the restored GitLab.com database.
Around 18:00 UTC we finished the final restoration procedures such as restoring the webhooks and confirming everything was operating as expected.

passos.texto: Projects created after 17:20 were restored from their Git repositories still stored in the NFS cluster, but only in their most basic form, without issues and merge requests.
trechos: We ran a procedure to restore these projects based on their Git repositories that were still stored in our NFS cluster.
This procedure however was only able to restore projects in their most basic form, without associated data such as issues and merge requests.

perguntas_em_aberto: The exact amount of lost data is hard to estimate; the text gives estimates of at least 5000 projects, 5000 comments and roughly 700 users.

motivo_confianca_baixa: categoria_causa: 'other' (root cause is the manual, unautomated and undocumented re-synchronisation procedure) vs 'human-error' (the destructive command run on the wrong host).
observacoes: The text gives two data-loss windows: changes between 17:20 and 00:00 UTC in the introduction, and between 17:20 and 23:30 UTC in the 'Data loss impact' section. It also says restoring GitLab.com took 'over 18 hours'; the stated 'about 18 hours' of downtime is used. The recovery plan's step of incrementing database sequences by 100,000 is given only as part of the planned process and is not confirmed as done.
